prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers, bringing optical time and frequency measurement to the 1e-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B038 to B042. In round 1 I kept trapped-ion gates first on originality and breadth, but I also wrote that I would accept the lattice clock if B038 could not be scoped narrowly against 2012. Having read all eight statements, I do not think it can be scoped well enough. Five colleagues independently press the same three points: Wineland and Monroe are outside the credited names, the label bundles ion computing with cold-atom simulation (where B050 is already on the list), and 2012 covers much of the ion-control ground. None of this changes my view that the Cirac-Zoller proposal is a deep idea, but a prize that I could not defend historically is a worse prize than one I can. B042 has the properties the statutes ask for: a specific invention (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice cancelling the light shift while holding many atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime), a decisive demonstration of its consequence (Ye's group at 1e-18, with redshift measurements over millimetres), independent reproduction in several laboratories and across fibre links, and a clean two-name credit. On the chair's question, I think the separation from 2005 and 2012 rests on one physical point: the stability gain from interrogating very many atoms at once with the light shift cancelled, which neither the comb nor single-ion clocks provide. The citation therefore names the lattice, the magic wavelength and the many-atom interrogation and says nothing about frequency metrology in general.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to my own new position is the one I used against others: overlap. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems sit under the lattice clock, and Ye's accuracy work leans on combs and ultrastable lasers, as Mehlig points out. A narrow citation answers this only if the committee accepts that the many-atom, magic-wavelength scheme is a separate invention and not an application of a honoured toolbox; a colleague may reasonably disagree. Second, the early-proposal and first-demonstration record has not been verified by anyone, including me, and Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others are outside the two names. A two-name credit that later proves to understate a priority claim would be hard to correct. Third, I remain convinced that quantum information, and the hardware platforms behind it, is the area where the physics has had the broadest reach in the last thirty years, and a B042 prize leaves that unrecognised for now. That is a reason to keep B038 as an alternative, not a reason to override the clearer case.

responses.point: Pearce asked how I would narrow a B038 citation, and argued that the 2012 overlap is stronger against B038 than the comb and ion-clock overlap is against B042, since a prize omitting Wineland and Monroe would be hard to defend historically.
responses.response: I tried to answer your question honestly. The narrowest defensible B038 citation is the gate proposal and its multi-ion realisation as a computational resource, leaving out cold-atom simulation and ion control in general. Even that version has to say something about Wineland's and Monroe's first demonstrated gate, and in three names there is no room for them without dropping Blatt. I could not write a citation that is both narrow and fair to the historical record, so I accept your argument and I am moving. I keep B038 as an alternative because the problem is the credit and the 2012 boundary, not the physics.

responses.point: Kroll agreed with my scoping of B038 to the gate proposal and its realisation, but said the ion-computing label is too broad and that the overlap with Wineland's group is exactly the difficulty; he places the lattice clock's boundary with 2005 and 2012 as cleaner.
responses.response: You answer the chair's question in a way I now accept. The decisive separation from 2005 and 2012 is the many-atom stability gain: a lattice of neutral atoms at the magic wavelength gives a signal-to-noise advantage that a single-ion clock cannot match, and the magic wavelength is what makes the trapping compatible with accuracy. I would put that in the citation explicitly. I would also ask you to carry your own Hall-laboratory disclosure into the wording check, since Ye's comb and ultrastable-laser work is the part of B042 closest to 2005, and you are better placed than I am to say whether it can be kept out of the credit.

responses.point: Lindroth pushed back on my seventh-place ranking of B042, saying that the overlap argument is stronger against B038 and B049 than against the lattice scheme, and that a citation worded around the lattice clock itself makes the 2005 exclusion visible.
responses.response: You were right to push back. My seventh place came from weighing breadth of influence above attribution, and the discussion has shown me that the weighting was wrong for this round. I agree on the wording and on not waiting for the redefinition. The one place I still differ is that the other early lattice-clock groups are a genuine open item; you list them as a concern too, and no one has checked the priority record. I would want that stated in our deliberation and not assumed away.

responses.point: Danielsson argued that my own caveats on B038 and B049 (2012 overlap, the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits) are an argument for placing B042 ahead of both, and that reach should not substitute for scientific distinctness.
responses.response: I agree with this reading of my own caveats, and the outcome of my changed ranking is that. I would qualify only the part about reach: I think industrial and scientific reach is relevant evidence of originality, but it does not repair a credit problem, and in B038 the credit problem is the binding one. On B057, which you place as your alternative, I share your attribution reservation and have kept it as my second alternative rather than a preferred part for that reason.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers DMFT (B033), lists B042 as an alternative, and regards the unfinished redefinition of the SI second as a reason for B042 to wait; he also noted that B033 has thin support and that Metzner is outside the credited trio.
responses.response: I do not think the redefinition should delay B042. The redefinition is a metrological and policy decision that rests on the clock comparisons already made; it is a consequence of the science, and the prize is for the science. On B033 I take your own list of reservations at face value: the support is thin, DMFT reads as a method and approximation scheme, and leaving out Metzner is a real hole in a three-name credit. My field is not yours, so I defer to you on the physics, but I could not support the configuration as drawn. I would be interested to know if you think a B033 citation can be written around the impurity mapping without that hole.

uncertainties: Whether the early lattice-clock proposal and first-demonstration record supports the Katori and Ye credit as written, given Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others; no member, including me, has verified it in detail.

Whether the committee will accept the many-atom magic-wavelength scheme as separable from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, given that Ye's accuracy results draw on comb and ultrastable-laser technology.
Whether recognising B042 now, before the SI second is redefined, is read as premature or as appropriately independent of metrological policy.

My own reading of lattice-clock physics is that of a neighbouring theorist, not a specialist in neutral-atom clocks, so I rely on Kroll and Lindroth for the details of the systematic-uncertainty budgets.
statement.conflict_note: My profile records no relationship with Katori or Ye, so no specific conflict is apparent for the preferred configuration. Updated disclosure: my change from B038 to B042 is not explained by my competing superconducting platform, but I note that WACQT's superconducting platform competes with trapped ions, so a possible bias against B038 remains disclosed, and I have therefore not tried to push that ballot past the arguments of colleagues. For the alternatives, B038 is the one with that bias, and I would remain restrained on any B049 (circuit QED) discussion: I direct WACQT at Chalmers, work on superconducting circuits and waveguide QED, and have documented Chalmers links to Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and co-author Anton Frisk Kockum. Olsson is also at Chalmers and has said she will not treat my views on circuit QED as independent; I accept that.
